original_value: This paper investigates countermeasures to side-channel attacks. A dynamic partial reconfiguration (DPR) method is proposed for field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs)s to make techniques such as differential power analysis (DPA) and correlation power analysis (CPA) difficult and ineffective. We call the technique side-channel power resistance for encryption algorithms using DPR, or SPREAD. SPREAD is designed to reduce cryptographic key related signal correlations in power supply transients by changing components of the hardware implementation on-the-fly using DPR. Replicated primitives within the advanced encryption standard (AES) algorithm, in particular, the substitution-box (SBOX)s, are synthesized to multiple and distinct gate-level implementations. The different implementations change the delay characteristics of the SBOXs, reducing correlations in the power traces, which, in turn, increases the difficulty of side-channel attacks. The effectiveness of the proposed countermeasures depends greatly on this principle; therefore, the focus of this paper is on the evaluation of implementation diversity techniques.

result.paraphrase: This paper examines defenses against side-channel attacks. It proposes a dynamic partial reconfiguration (DPR) approach for field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) to make methods such as differential power analysis (DPA) and correlation power analysis (CPA) more difficult and less effective. The technique is named side-channel power resistance for encryption algorithms using DPR, or SPREAD. SPREAD aims to cut signal correlations tied to cryptographic keys in power-supply transients by altering parts of the hardware implementation on the fly through DPR. Within the advanced encryption standard (AES) algorithm, replicated primitives—especially the substitution-boxes (SBOXs)—are synthesized into multiple, distinct gate-level implementations. By changing SBOX delay characteristics, these implementations reduce correlations in power traces and thereby raise the difficulty of side-channel attacks. Since the proposed countermeasures rely heavily on this principle, the paper focuses on evaluating implementation diversity techniques.
